Keywords: Coastal Salt Pans and Meat Brining
RagShortTexts: Salt was essential for winter meat preservation, exploited by royal gabelle tax monopolies.

Variants.Content: Salt was essential for curing meat and salting herring through the winter, which made it the most sought-after commodity in Europe. Monarchs turned it into a source of revenue by creating state monopolies. The French gabelle required each household to buy a fixed quota of salt from royal storehouses, the greniers a sel, at prices set well above the cost of production. The money filled the standing treasuries that paid for armies and officials. Because every family needed salt, the tax reached the poorest households in the land.

Coastal salt pans, such as those at Chioggia for Venice or Hyeres in Provence, gave their owners dependable income. That income paid for war fleets and diplomatic bribes, so a lord who held a lagoon or saltworks could finance a campaign without waiting on his king. Control of salt was control of the purse.

Official salt is gray, gritty, and exorbitant. Despite brutal gallows penalties for smuggling (faux-saunage), highland runners risk everything to pack untaxed sea salt through nocturnal mountain trails.
